moments.title: Priestley isolates 'dephlogisticated air'
moments.body:
Priestley focuses sunlight through a lens onto mercuric oxide in a glass vessel. A gas evolves. He breathes it and reports feeling 'peculiarly light and easy'. A mouse placed in it survives longer than in normal air.

He believes air contains 'phlogiston' — a fire-substance released by burning. His new gas is 'air from which phlogiston has been removed', and so eagerly accepts more phlogiston (i.e., supports combustion and respiration).

quote.text: Who can tell but that, in time, this pure air may become a fashionable article in luxury.
quote.attrib: Joseph Priestley, Experiments and Observations on Different Kinds of Air, 1775

moments.takeaway: Priestley discovers oxygen but interprets it backwards through the phlogiston framework.

moments.title: Priestley visits Paris and tells Lavoisier
moments.body:
Lavoisier had been measuring masses before and after combustion — meticulously. When metals burned, they GAINED weight. Phlogiston theory had no answer: how can losing phlogiston make you heavier?

Priestley described his new gas at a dinner with Lavoisier. Within months, Lavoisier was repeating the experiments and reframing them: combustion is the COMBINATION of substances with this new gas, which he named oxygen ('acid-forming', in Greek).
moments.takeaway: Quantitative measurement broke phlogiston theory. The same gas, two interpretations, only one survives.

moments.title: Lavoisier's Traité Élémentaire de Chimie
moments.body:
Lavoisier publishes the first modern chemistry textbook. He defines an element as a substance that cannot be broken down by chemical means. He lists 33 elements (including caloric and light, which we now know aren't). He insists chemistry must be a quantitative science — mass conservation is its central law.

He also gives modern names: oxygen, hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, sulphur. Most are still in use.

quote.text: Nothing is lost, nothing is created — everything is transformed.
quote.attrib: Antoine Lavoisier, paraphrased — the law of conservation of mass

moments.takeaway: Lavoisier reorganises chemistry around mass balance. Modern chemistry begins here.

moments.title: Lavoisier guillotined during the Terror
moments.body:
Lavoisier had worked as a tax collector for the ancien régime — the Ferme générale, profitable but loathed. On 8 May 1794 he was tried and executed by guillotine during the Reign of Terror.

The mathematician Lagrange remarked: 'It took them only a moment to cut off his head; a hundred years will not suffice to produce another like it.'
moments.takeaway: The father of modern chemistry was killed at age 50 in a political purge.

now.title: Where we are now
now.body:
Oxygen is the third most abundant element in the universe (after hydrogen and helium) and the most abundant in Earth's crust by mass (about 46 percent). Cellular respiration, combustion engines, steelmaking and rocket fuel all hinge on it.

The paramagnetism of O2 — which puzzled chemists for decades — was finally explained by molecular orbital theory. Allotropes (O2, O3, O4) and singlet oxygen are now routine.
now.open_questions: How did Earth's atmosphere become 21 percent oxygen? (Answer: cyanobacterial photosynthesis starting 2.4 billion years ago, the 'Great Oxidation Event'.) Why is Earth one of the few known oxygen-rich planets? Could oxygen-based biology arise on planets with very different histories?

items.reflection: Priestley named his gas backwards — 'dephlogisticated air' — and never accepted Lavoisier's oxygen theory. He died in 1804 still defending phlogiston. How should the history of science treat a discoverer who refuses to accept the implications of their own discovery?

moments.title: The Karlsruhe Congress
moments.body:
Chemistry in 1860 has no agreed atomic masses. The same element gets different values in different labs. Stanislao Cannizzaro distributes a pamphlet at the Karlsruhe Congress that revives Avogadro's hypothesis and gives consistent atomic masses.

Among the delegates: a 26-year-old Russian named Dmitri Mendeleev. He reads Cannizzaro's pamphlet and starts trying to organise the elements.
moments.takeaway: Without agreed atomic masses, no periodic table was possible. Karlsruhe gave chemistry a foundation.

moments.title: Mendeleev's first periodic table
moments.body:
Mendeleev is writing a chemistry textbook. He sketches out the 63 known elements in order of atomic mass and notices that similar properties recur regularly. He published his table in the journal of the Russian Chemical Society in March 1869.

Mendeleev's audacity: where his pattern required an element that didn't exist, he LEFT A GAP and predicted its properties.

quote.text: We must expect the discovery of many yet unknown elements — for example, two analogues of boron and aluminium with atomic weights 65 and 75.
quote.attrib: Mendeleev, 1871

moments.takeaway: Mendeleev didn't just classify what was known — he predicted what wasn't.

moments.title: Gallium, scandium, germanium
moments.body:
Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovers gallium spectroscopically (1875). Its properties match Mendeleev's predicted 'eka-aluminium' almost exactly — including atomic mass 69.7 (predicted 68), density 5.9 (predicted 5.9), and forming a 3+ chloride.

Scandium (1879) matches 'eka-boron'. Germanium (1886) matches 'eka-silicon'. Three predictions, three confirmations within Mendeleev's lifetime.
moments.takeaway: Predicting unknown elements transformed Mendeleev's table from a classification into a scientific theory.

moments.title: Moseley reorders by atomic number
moments.body:
Mendeleev had ordered elements by atomic mass, but the order felt 'wrong' in places (tellurium before iodine, despite tellurium being heavier). Henry Moseley measured the X-ray spectra of elements and showed each element has a characteristic 'atomic number' (proton count) that gives the true sequence.

Moseley was killed at Gallipoli in 1915, aged 27. His death prompted the British government to restrict young scientists from front-line combat.

quote.text: Now the elements can be examined one by one in their proper order, even when the atomic weights make hash of the order.
quote.attrib: Henry Moseley, 1913

moments.takeaway: Atomic number, not mass, is the periodic table's true organising principle.

now.title: The table today
now.body:
118 elements are now confirmed — the last (oganesson) named in 2016. Synthesis of superheavy elements happens at heavy-ion colliders in Dubna (Russia), GSI (Germany), and Berkeley (USA), one or a few atoms at a time.

The periodic table's structure is explained by quantum mechanics: shells, subshells and electron configurations. Mendeleev's empirical patterns are direct consequences of orbital filling rules.
now.open_questions: How far can the table extend? Predictions of an 'island of stability' near element 114 or 126 suggest some superheavy elements might be (relatively) stable. Element 119 has been searched for since 2007 but never confirmed. Is there a fundamental upper limit to atomic number?

items.reflection: Mendeleev was passed over for the Nobel Prize in 1906 (by one vote, in favour of Henri Moissan for isolating fluorine). He died in 1907. How should scientific recognition deal with achievements that pre-date the prize?

moments.title: Dalton's atomic theory
moments.body:
Dalton, a Quaker schoolteacher with no university post, presents a paper proposing that elements are made of indivisible atoms. Different elements have atoms of different mass. Compounds form by simple integer ratios of atoms.

He uses the law of multiple proportions (carbon and oxygen form CO with 1:1 mass ratio and CO2 with 1:2) as evidence.

quote.text: We might as well attempt to introduce a new planet into the solar system, or annihilate one already in existence, as to create or destroy a particle of hydrogen.
quote.attrib: John Dalton

moments.takeaway: Dalton's atoms are indivisible billiard balls. This is the first quantitative atomic theory of modern science.

moments.title: Thomson discovers the electron
moments.who: J. J. Thomson, Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge
moments.body:
Cathode rays — glowing streams in evacuated tubes — were known but mysterious. Thomson shows they consist of negatively charged particles with charge-to-mass ratio about 1000 times that of hydrogen ions.

The particles are the same regardless of which gas is in the tube or which metal makes the cathode. Thomson proposes they are sub-atomic — pieces of all atoms.

quote.text: I have been driven to the conclusion that they are charges of negative electricity carried by particles of matter.
quote.attrib: J. J. Thomson, 1897

moments.takeaway: The atom is no longer the smallest thing. Dalton's billiard ball has internal structure.

moments.title: Rutherford's gold foil experiment
moments.body:
Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil. Most pass through, as expected from Thomson's 'plum pudding' model (positive charge spread out, with electrons embedded). But about 1 in 8000 bounce backwards.

Rutherford described his reaction: 'It was as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.'

The data force a new model: positive charge is concentrated in a tiny dense nucleus, with electrons orbiting at a distance.
moments.takeaway: The atom is mostly empty space. A dense nucleus, surrounded by electrons at huge relative distance.

moments.title: Bohr's quantised orbits
moments.body:
Classical electromagnetism predicts orbiting electrons should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus. They don't. Hydrogen's emission spectrum has discrete lines, not a continuous spectrum.

Bohr proposes electrons orbit in 'quantised' orbits — only specific radii allowed, only specific energies. Jumping between orbits emits a photon of frequency f = (E1 - E2)/h.

The theory reproduces hydrogen's Rydberg formula exactly. It also has obvious flaws — it doesn't work for any other atom.
moments.takeaway: Quantisation is in. The classical picture of orbits is on borrowed time.

moments.title: Schrödinger's wave equation
moments.body:
Schrödinger writes down a wave equation governing the electron's wavefunction. Solving for hydrogen gives orbitals (s, p, d, f) — not classical orbits but probability distributions.

Heisenberg's matrix mechanics (1925) gives an equivalent picture. The Pauli exclusion principle (1925) explains why electrons fill shells. Quantum mechanics becomes the foundation of modern chemistry.

quote.text: I don't like it, and I'm sorry I ever had anything to do with it.
quote.attrib: Erwin Schrödinger, on the probabilistic interpretation of his own equation

moments.takeaway: Atoms are governed by wavefunctions, not orbits. Chemistry is quantum mechanics applied to electrons in fields of nuclei.

now.title: Atoms today
now.body:
The atom is made of a nucleus (protons and neutrons) and a cloud of electrons described by wavefunctions. Protons and neutrons are themselves made of quarks (up and down) bound by gluons. Quantum chromodynamics describes that level.

We can image individual atoms (scanning tunnelling microscope, 1981), trap single atoms in lasers, and manipulate them with optical tweezers (2018 Nobel).
now.open_questions: Is there a deeper structure inside quarks? The Standard Model has 17 fundamental particles — why these specifically? Why are there three families of matter? Why is the electron mass exactly what it is?

items.reflection: Dalton was colour-blind (the first scientific description of colour blindness, by Dalton himself). He never knew sodium emits yellow light because he couldn't see yellow. How does a researcher's perceptual world shape what they choose to investigate?

moments.title: Faraday isolates benzene
moments.body:
Faraday is investigating illuminating gas produced from whale oil for street lighting. He distils and analyses an oily liquid, finding a hydrogen-to-carbon ratio of 1:1. He calls it 'bicarburet of hydrogen'.

The formula is right but its structure is a complete mystery. How can a molecule with so few hydrogens (relative to carbons) be stable?
moments.takeaway: Benzene is isolated; its structure becomes one of organic chemistry's central problems.

moments.title: Chemists struggle with C6H6
moments.body:
The known carbon valence of 4 doesn't permit a C6H6 structure with single bonds (would need C6H14). Multiple bonds were known but using three or more in such a small molecule seemed implausible to many.

Josef Loschmidt (1861) drew a circular structure for benzene — close to modern depictions — but his book was obscure and ignored. Archibald Couper proposed structural formulas based on bond connectivity but his work was suppressed.
moments.takeaway: The right answer was sometimes proposed and ignored. Scientific consensus takes more than a correct paper.

moments.title: Kekulé's snake dream
moments.body:
Kekulé publishes the ring structure for benzene: six carbons in a hexagonal ring with alternating single and double bonds. He later told a story (at the 25th anniversary celebration in 1890) of having dozed by a fire and dreamed of atoms dancing as snakes, one of which seized its own tail and 'whirled mockingly before my eyes'.

Historians have questioned whether the dream story is true or a rhetorical flourish 25 years later. The structure itself, however, opened the door to aromatic chemistry.

quote.text: Let us learn to dream, gentlemen, and then perhaps we shall find the truth.
quote.attrib: August Kekulé, 1890 speech

moments.takeaway: Kekulé's hexagonal ring with alternating bonds becomes the structural cornerstone of organic chemistry — even if the dream story is dramatised.

moments.title: Pauling's resonance theory
moments.body:
X-ray diffraction shows all benzene C-C bonds are equal length (139 pm) — not alternating single and double bonds as Kekulé drew them.

Pauling proposes resonance: the real molecule is a quantum superposition of the two Kekulé structures, with delocalised pi electrons. The double-headed arrow becomes a key symbol of organic chemistry.
moments.takeaway: Bonds in benzene are not alternating single/double — they are an average. Quantum mechanics formalises what the molecule actually is.

now.title: Aromaticity in modern chemistry
now.body:
Aromaticity now generalises far beyond benzene. Hückel's rule (4n+2 pi electrons in a planar ring) covers furan, pyrrole, naphthalene and porphyrins. Anti-aromatic compounds (4n electrons) are destabilised. Aromaticity drives the structure of DNA bases, chlorophyll, haem and most drugs.

Materials made of aromatic carbon networks (graphene, carbon nanotubes, fullerenes) now form a major research area.
now.open_questions: Can we design new classes of aromatic systems for organic electronics or solar cells? What's the limit of stability for super-large polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (found in interstellar space)? How do biological systems exploit aromaticity in unexpected ways (light harvesting, electron transport)?

items.reflection: Kekulé and his contemporaries assigned structures BEFORE atoms were widely accepted as physical reality. They were inferring shape from chemical behaviour, without direct evidence atoms existed. How do scientists work confidently with constructs they cannot see?

moments.title: Becquerel discovers radioactivity
moments.body:
Becquerel wraps a uranium-containing salt in black paper next to photographic plates. Even without sunlight, the plates are exposed. Uranium emits its own penetrating radiation.

It's a chance discovery — Becquerel had been testing whether phosphorescent minerals could emit X-rays after sunlight exposure. Cloudy weather forced him to put the experiment in a drawer; the plates developed anyway.
moments.takeaway: Some elements spontaneously emit radiation. Nothing in chemistry to date predicted this.

moments.title: The Curies isolate polonium and radium
moments.body:
Marie Curie uses an electrometer her husband helped design to measure radiation precisely. She finds pitchblende (uranium ore) is more radioactive than uranium alone — there must be something more radioactive in it.

They process tonnes of pitchblende in a leaky shed. They isolate first polonium (named for Marie's native Poland), then radium. Radium is intensely radioactive, glowing in the dark.

quote.text: Radium ought to enrich no one. It is an element; it belongs to the people.
quote.attrib: Marie Curie, on refusing to patent her isolation process

moments.takeaway: Two new elements, both highly radioactive. The Curies refuse to patent — and remain poor.

moments.title: Nobel Prize in Physics
moments.body:
Marie Curie is the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. The original nominations had named only Becquerel and Pierre. Pierre wrote to the committee insisting Marie be included.

They were too ill from radiation exposure to travel to Stockholm. Marie's notebooks remain radioactive today — they're stored in lead boxes and visitors must wear protective equipment to handle them.
moments.takeaway: Recognition for the discovery — and the first formal demonstration of the dangers of intense radioactivity, even if not yet understood.

moments.title: Hahn, Strassmann and Meitner — nuclear fission
moments.who: Otto Hahn, Fritz Strassmann (Berlin), Lise Meitner (in exile in Sweden)
moments.body:
Hahn and Strassmann bombard uranium with neutrons and detect barium in the products — about half the mass of uranium. Hahn writes to Lise Meitner (an Austrian Jew who had fled Nazi Germany the previous year) asking for an explanation.

Meitner and her nephew Otto Frisch realise: the uranium nucleus has SPLIT. They calculate the energy released using Einstein's E = mc squared — about 200 MeV per fission. They name the process 'fission' by analogy with bacterial cell division.
moments.takeaway: Atoms can split, releasing enormous energy. The nuclear age begins.

moments.title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
moments.body:
Less than 7 years after fission was discovered, atomic bombs were used on civilian cities. Between 90,000 and 200,000 people died in the immediate explosions and subsequent radiation sickness.

Meitner refused to work on the Manhattan Project. Hahn was interned in England when the bombs fell and was deeply affected. Many physicists who had worked on the bomb spent their later lives campaigning against nuclear weapons.
moments.takeaway: Pure science has consequences that scientists cannot fully control.

now.title: Nuclear chemistry today
now.body:
Radioactive isotopes are used in medical imaging (PET, SPECT) and therapy (cobalt-60, iodine-131). Carbon-14 dating reveals archaeological ages. Nuclear power provides about 10 percent of global electricity. Nuclear weapons remain a geopolitical concern, with around 12,000 warheads worldwide.

We understand alpha, beta and gamma decay, fission, fusion, isotope separation and reactor design. ITER (under construction in France) aims for sustained fusion power by the 2030s.
now.open_questions: Can fusion become practical for grid-scale electricity? How safe can fission reactor designs be made (small modular reactors, molten salt reactors)? What's the long-term solution for nuclear waste? Why do certain neutron-to-proton ratios produce stable nuclei (the 'magic numbers')?

items.reflection: Marie Curie died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia, almost certainly caused by her decades of radiation exposure. She kept radium samples in her desk drawer. She was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes in different sciences (Physics 1903, Chemistry 1911). How does a discipline reckon with discoveries whose dangers were only learned at the cost of the discoverers' lives?

moments.title: Baekeland's Bakelite
moments.body:
Baekeland heats phenol with formaldehyde under pressure. The product is hard, mouldable when warm, then sets into a permanently rigid solid. It's the first fully synthetic plastic — not derived from any natural material.

Bakelite is used for telephones, radio cabinets, electrical insulators, jewellery, automotive parts. Baekeland founds a company and becomes very rich.
moments.takeaway: Synthetic polymers enter the world. Plastic begins.

moments.title: Staudinger insists polymers are LONG molecules
moments.body:
Chemists in the 1920s think materials like rubber and cellulose are aggregates of small molecules — colloidal clusters held together loosely. Staudinger insists they are actual giant covalent molecules ('macromolecules'), with thousands of atoms joined by ordinary chemical bonds.

The idea is mocked. Leading chemists tell him to stop being ridiculous. Staudinger pushes back with viscosity measurements showing rubber's behaviour matches that of single long-chain molecules.

quote.text: Out of respect for our science, my dear colleague, abandon this idea of large molecules; organic molecules with molecular weights above 5000 do not exist.
quote.attrib: Senior German chemist to Staudinger, 1926

moments.takeaway: Staudinger is right; the chemistry establishment is wrong. Macromolecules become accepted, and he wins the 1953 Nobel Prize.

moments.title: Wallace Carothers invents nylon
moments.body:
Carothers leads a basic-research group at DuPont. He systematically synthesises long-chain polyamides and polyesters, looking for fibres. On 28 February 1935, his team makes nylon-6,6 from adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine — the first fully synthetic fibre.

Nylon stockings go on sale in 1940. Lines form around the block. During WWII, nylon goes to parachutes, ropes and tyres instead.
moments.takeaway: Synthetic fibres are born. Carothers had specifically targeted a useful fibre and got one.

moments.title: Carothers takes his own life
moments.body:
Carothers had suffered from depression for years. He carried cyanide in a capsule. On 28 April 1937, two days after his 41st birthday and shortly after the death of his sister, he ingested it at a Philadelphia hotel.

He never saw nylon sold commercially. His patent on nylon was issued in September 1938. DuPont's profits from nylon ran into billions of dollars.
moments.takeaway: Carothers received his greatest professional recognition posthumously.

now.title: Plastics now
now.body:
Global plastic production exceeds 400 million tonnes per year. Polyethylene, polypropylene, polystyrene, PET, PVC dominate everyday use. Specialty polymers (Kevlar, PEEK, conductive polymers, biodegradable PLA) extend the range.

We understand polymerisation mechanisms (chain growth, step growth, living polymerisation, ATRP), structural control (stereoregularity from Ziegler-Natta catalysts) and the relationship between molecular structure and macroscopic properties.
now.open_questions: How do we deal with plastic pollution at scale? Can chemical recycling (depolymerisation back to monomers) compete with virgin plastic on cost? Can fully biodegradable polymers replace persistent ones without losing performance? Why does microplastic accumulate in living tissues, and what are the consequences?

items.reflection: Carothers worked on basic science but produced a transformative consumer product. He didn't choose his projects for commercial impact, yet they reshaped global manufacturing and daily life. How should research be funded when the connection between curiosity-driven work and society-altering applications is impossible to predict?

moments.title: Cavendish notices a residue
moments.body:
Cavendish passes electric sparks through air to combine its nitrogen and oxygen into nitric oxide. He absorbs the products with alkali. A small bubble — about 1/120th of the original air — refuses to react.

Cavendish notes this in passing and moves on. The residue is unidentified for over a century.
moments.takeaway: An anomalous finding sits unexplained for 109 years. Science accumulates loose threads.

moments.title: Rayleigh and Ramsay isolate argon
moments.who: Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay, Cambridge and London
moments.body:
Rayleigh notices that nitrogen extracted from air is denser than nitrogen made from chemical compounds, by 0.5 percent. Ramsay suggests there's a heavier contaminant in atmospheric nitrogen.

They remove all nitrogen by passing the gas over hot magnesium, leaving a residue that won't react with anything they throw at it. Spectroscopy reveals an unfamiliar emission spectrum. They call it argon ('the lazy one' in Greek). It makes up about 1 percent of air.

quote.text: The new gas has so far failed to combine with any other substance.
quote.attrib: Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay, 1895

moments.takeaway: A new element is hiding in plain sight, in the air everyone breathes.

moments.title: The noble gas family
moments.body:
Ramsay discovers helium on Earth in 1895 (it had been identified from solar spectrum lines in 1868 but not isolated terrestrially). In 1898 he and Morris Travers liquify air and distil out three more: krypton, neon and xenon.

Mendeleev's periodic table has no place for an entire new family. Mendeleev initially resists. Then he and Ramsay agree: the noble gases form a new group (Group 0, now Group 18). The table is extended.
moments.takeaway: A whole new column of the periodic table appears in five years. Existing organising structures can absorb major surprises.

moments.title: Bartlett breaks the noble gases' inertness
moments.who: Neil Bartlett, University of British Columbia
moments.body:
Bartlett is working with platinum hexafluoride, an extraordinarily strong oxidiser. He notices a sample turns red on contact with air. He realises PtF6 has stripped an electron from oxygen to form O2+ PtF6-.

Looking at ionisation energies: O2's first ionisation is 1175 kJ/mol; xenon's is 1170. Almost the same. He tries XePtF6 — and it works. The first noble gas compound exists.

quote.text: I had to look twice to believe it.
quote.attrib: Neil Bartlett, on the first XePtF6 product

moments.takeaway: Noble gases aren't inert after all. The right oxidiser opens up an entire new chemistry.

now.title: Noble gases today
now.body:
Helium is critical for MRI machine cooling, supersonic wind tunnels, gas chromatography and cryogenics. Argon fills incandescent bulbs and shields TIG welding. Neon glows in advertising signs. Krypton and xenon are used in headlamps, ion thrusters and lasers. Radon is a hazard in some basements (radioactive product of uranium decay).

Xenon and krypton have rich fluoride and oxide chemistry. Argon and helium remain genuinely unreactive in normal conditions — but ArF and HArF have been made at cryogenic temperatures.
now.open_questions: Can the lightest noble gases (helium, neon) ever form stable compounds in normal conditions? Why is helium becoming scarce on Earth (it leaks into space), and how should it be conserved? Recent finds: Boncuk gas field in Tanzania discovered helium reserves in 2022.

items.reflection: Mendeleev's periodic table did not predict the noble gases — they were not 'missing' from his sequence. He had to adapt. How do scientific theories accommodate genuinely unexpected categories of phenomena, and what does it tell us about predictive power?

moments.title: The doctrine of vital force
moments.body:
Most chemists in the 1820s believe organic compounds (those found in living things) require a 'vital force' to be made. You can decompose them in the lab, but you cannot synthesise them from inorganic precursors. Living organisms are the only source.

The view goes back to ancient Greek philosophy and was articulated formally by Berzelius. It draws a line between organic and inorganic chemistry that seems unbridgeable.
moments.takeaway: A widely accepted boundary separates 'living' chemistry from 'mineral' chemistry.

moments.title: Wöhler makes urea
moments.body:
Wöhler is trying to make ammonium cyanate (NH4CNO) from silver cyanate and ammonium chloride. The product crystallises out as colourless prisms. Wöhler tests its properties: it is identical to urea, the organic substance excreted by mammals.

He writes to Berzelius: 'I can make urea without the use of kidneys, either man or dog.'

quote.text: I must tell you that I can prepare urea without requiring a kidney of an animal, either man or dog.
quote.attrib: Friedrich Wöhler, letter to Berzelius, 1828

moments.takeaway: An organic substance is made from inorganic precursors. The vital force doctrine starts to crack.

moments.title: More organic syntheses
moments.body:
Wöhler's synthesis was striking but isolated — urea is unusual in being a 'simple' organic compound. Later syntheses are unambiguous.

Kolbe synthesises acetic acid from carbon disulfide and chlorine (1845). Berthelot synthesises methanol, ethanol, methane, acetylene and benzene from inorganic precursors (1850s-1860s) and publishes Chimie Organique Fondée sur la Synthèse in 1860 — a deliberate manifesto against vitalism.

By 1870 vitalism is no longer scientifically respectable.
moments.takeaway: Organic chemistry becomes the chemistry of carbon, not the chemistry of life.

moments.title: Miller-Urey synthesise amino acids from gases
moments.who: Stanley Miller and Harold Urey, Chicago
moments.body:
Miller (a graduate student) and Urey (his supervisor) build an apparatus simulating Earth's early atmosphere: methane, ammonia, hydrogen, water, with electrical discharges as 'lightning'.

After a week of running the spark, the water turns brown. Analysis shows several amino acids — glycine, alanine and others — formed from purely inorganic starting materials. One of the foundational building blocks of life had been synthesised from a 'lifeless' mixture.
moments.takeaway: Not just organic compounds — biologically essential organic compounds — can form spontaneously without life.

now.title: Organic chemistry today
now.body:
Organic synthesis is a dominant branch of chemistry: pharmaceuticals, materials, agrochemicals, natural products. Total synthesis of complex molecules (Taxol, palytoxin, vitamin B12) showcases the field's reach.

We routinely synthesise molecules that have never existed in nature, and modify natural products to engineer new properties. AI-assisted retrosynthesis is now competitive with experienced chemists at planning synthesis routes.
now.open_questions: Can we synthesise every conceivable organic molecule? (Probably not — the chemical space is too large.) Can we synthesise life itself from non-living precursors? (Craig Venter's lab built a synthetic genome in 2010; full synthetic cells remain a goal.) What molecules in space (interstellar medium, Titan, comets) chart organic chemistry under non-Earth conditions?

items.reflection: Wöhler's 1828 synthesis is sometimes presented as the single death blow to vitalism. Historians of science have argued the reality was more gradual — vitalism declined over decades as more syntheses accumulated. How do we deal with the human desire for tidy 'moments of revolution' in stories of science?

moments.title: Payen and Persoz isolate diastase
moments.who: Anselme Payen and Jean-François Persoz, Paris
moments.body:
They extract a substance from malt that converts starch into sugar. They call it diastase ('separation' in Greek). It's the first isolated enzyme — though they don't know what they have.

For decades enzymes are treated as mysterious 'ferments' — substances that act without being consumed, but whose nature is unclear.
moments.takeaway: Cells contain catalysts. We don't yet understand what they are.

moments.title: Emil Fischer's lock and key
moments.body:
Fischer is studying sugar chemistry. He finds different enzymes act on different sugar stereoisomers — emulsin cleaves alpha-glycosides; invertase cleaves beta-glycosides. He proposes enzymes have a specific shape that fits their substrates.

Fischer's analogy: lock and key. Only the right key fits.

quote.text: To use a picture I will say that enzyme and glucoside must fit into each other like a lock and key.
quote.attrib: Emil Fischer, 1894

moments.takeaway: Catalytic specificity comes from molecular shape. The seeds of structural biology.

moments.title: Sumner crystallises urease
moments.body:
Until 1926, leading biochemists (notably Richard Willstätter) insist enzymes are not proteins — proteins are too 'simple' to have catalytic activity.

Sumner crystallises urease from jack beans and shows it's a pure protein, fully catalytically active. The biochemical community largely ignores him. By the mid-1930s, more enzymes have been crystallised and shown to be proteins, and Sumner's work is accepted. He gets the 1946 Nobel Prize.
moments.takeaway: Enzymes are proteins. Even Nobel-Prize-winning insights have to fight resistance.

moments.title: Koshland's induced fit
moments.body: Fischer's lock-and-key model can't explain why some 'small' molecules fit certain enzymes that 'should' have room for them but don't react. Koshland proposes the enzyme CHANGES SHAPE when it binds the right substrate — induced fit. Wrong substrates don't trigger the conformational change and don't react.
moments.takeaway: Enzymes are dynamic. They don't just hold substrates — they reorganise around them.

moments.title: First protein structure — lysozyme
moments.who: David Phillips and team, Royal Institution, London
moments.body:
Phillips and colleagues solve the X-ray crystal structure of hen egg-white lysozyme at 2.0 angstrom resolution. It's the first enzyme structure ever determined.

They can see the active site, model substrate binding and propose a mechanism — making physical sense of decades of kinetic data.
moments.takeaway: We can now see enzymes at atomic resolution. Biochemistry becomes structural biology.

now.title: Enzymes today
now.body:
Over 7,000 enzymes are catalogued. Their structures (more than 200,000 in the Protein Data Bank) are routinely solved by X-ray crystallography or cryo-electron microscopy. AlphaFold (DeepMind, 2020) predicts protein structures with near-experimental accuracy.

We engineer enzymes for industrial use (laundry detergent proteases, cellulose breakdown for biofuels, drug synthesis). Frances Arnold won the 2018 Nobel Prize for directed evolution — letting selection design enzymes for us.
now.open_questions: Can we design enzymes from scratch (de novo) for any reaction we want? How do enzymes achieve rate accelerations of 10 to the 17 or more compared to uncatalysed reactions? Why are so many enzyme structures conserved across billion-year evolutionary timescales?

items.reflection: Sumner's discovery that enzymes are proteins was rejected by the leading biochemist of the day (Willstätter, a Nobel laureate). For 8 years the community sided with the famous man over the right one. How does science recover from situations where authority overrides evidence?

moments.title: Boyle's chemistry of fire
moments.body:
Boyle establishes that combustion needs air. He shows a candle in a sealed jar goes out, and a mouse in the same jar suffocates. He concludes air contains something essential to burning and breathing.

He does not name the substance. The Sceptical Chymist (1661) is a manifesto for chemistry as an experimental discipline.
moments.takeaway: Boyle frames burning as a chemical process needing a specific component of air.

moments.title: Stahl's phlogiston theory
moments.body:
Stahl unifies combustion, calcination of metals and respiration under one concept: all involve release of a hypothetical substance called phlogiston. Combustible materials are rich in phlogiston; non-combustible materials lack it.

The theory works coherently for most observations — until people start weighing things carefully.
moments.takeaway: Phlogiston unifies fire, rust and breathing. A productive but ultimately wrong theory.

moments.title: Lavoisier's sealed-vessel experiments
moments.body:
Lavoisier conducts a deposition: 'I deposit the following note... so that I can claim its discovery as my own if others should make the same observations.' He had noted: a metal calcined in a sealed vessel does not change the total weight; on opening the vessel, air rushes in, and the metal's calx weighs more than the original metal.

The weight gained equals the air that rushed in. Burning ADDS mass from air — it doesn't release phlogiston.
moments.takeaway: Quantitative observation overturns a major theory. Lavoisier is staking a claim.

moments.title: Lavoisier announces the new theory
moments.body:
Lavoisier publishes 'Réflexions sur le Phlogistique', a full attack on phlogiston theory. Combustion is the combination of substances with oxygen. The decrease in air volume during burning equals the oxygen consumed.

The old guard resists. Priestley dies in 1804 still defending phlogiston. By 1810 phlogiston is dead among working chemists.
moments.takeaway: A scientific revolution takes about 25 years to be accepted, despite clean experimental evidence.

now.title: Combustion today
now.body:
We understand combustion at multiple levels. Macroscopic: fuel + oxygen → CO2 + H2O + energy. Detailed: hundreds of elementary radical reactions, modelled by chemical kinetics software. Internal combustion engines, jet engines, rockets — all designed using combustion chemistry.

Low-temperature combustion (HCCI engines), oxy-fuel combustion (for carbon capture), hydrogen combustion (water as the only product) are active research areas.
now.open_questions: Can we capture CO2 at the point of combustion at scale and at low cost? Can hydrogen replace fossil fuels in industrial-scale combustion? How do soot and aerosol particles form and what's their full climate impact?

items.reflection: Stahl's phlogiston theory was wrong but useful for nearly a century. It made predictions and could be tested. Lavoisier's theory replaced it because of mass measurements that Stahl's contemporaries couldn't have made. How do we treat theories that are 'productively wrong' in their own time?

moments.title: Arrhenius's dissociation theory
moments.body:
Arrhenius proposes for his PhD that salts in water dissociate into ions. Acids release H+. Bases release OH-. Neutralisation is H+ + OH- → H2O.

The Uppsala examiners gave him a low-pass grade. Some considered him a crank. The theory turned out to be correct (within its domain) and earned him the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
moments.takeaway: Acids and bases get a molecular-level definition. Reception is grudging.

moments.title: Sørensen introduces pH
moments.who: S. P. L. Sørensen, Carlsberg Laboratory, Copenhagen
moments.body:
Sørensen is studying enzyme catalysis at the Carlsberg brewing labs. He introduces the symbol pH for the negative log of hydrogen-ion concentration. The notation makes the wide range of [H+] (from about 1 M to 10 to the minus 14 M) manageable.

pH = 7 is neutral. pH < 7 acidic. pH > 7 alkaline. The scale is logarithmic — pH 4 is ten times more acidic than pH 5.
moments.takeaway: A practical scale for everyday and lab chemistry, born in a brewery.

moments.title: Brønsted and Lowry generalise acid-base
moments.body:
Arrhenius's theory only works in water and only for substances that release H+ or OH-. Many obvious acid-base reactions (in liquid ammonia, or with substances like NH3 acting as a base) don't fit.

Brønsted and Lowry propose: acids donate protons, bases accept them. The definition extends to all solvents and to gas-phase reactions. The same year Lewis proposes an even broader definition based on electron-pair donation/acceptance.
moments.takeaway: Acid-base chemistry generalises beyond water. Definitions evolve to fit experimental scope.

moments.title: Lewis's electron pair theory wins ground
moments.body:
Lewis had proposed (1923) that acids accept electron pairs, bases donate them. The definition includes substances like BF3 (an acid by Lewis but not by Brønsted) and embraces all of coordination chemistry.

The Brønsted-Lowry and Lewis definitions coexist. Most aqueous chemistry uses Brønsted. Organic and inorganic mechanisms often use Lewis.
moments.takeaway: Different definitions illuminate different chemistry. Acid-base is a hierarchy of generalisations.

now.title: Acids and bases today
now.body:
We measure pH to better than 0.01 units with glass electrodes. Buffers stabilise pH in biological systems (blood at 7.4) and industrial processes. Superacids (like fluoroantimonic acid, HSbF6, 10 to the 19 times stronger than 100 percent sulfuric acid) protonate alkanes; superbases pull protons off C-H bonds.

Biochemistry tracks proton movements as the universal currency of energy (chemiosmosis), signal (pH-sensing receptors), and synthesis (DNA polymerase requires Mg2+ and proper pH).
now.open_questions: What's the most acidic possible substance? (No theoretical upper limit, but synthesis is hard.) How do biological systems achieve the pH gradients they need without short-circuiting? Can pH-responsive smart materials replace mechanical control in microfluidics?

items.reflection: Arrhenius's PhD thesis was awarded the lowest possible pass grade. Within 20 years it had become Nobel-winning work. How do we evaluate radical work when the established standards don't yet apply?

moments.title: Tswett invents chromatography
moments.body:
Mikhail Tswett, a Russian-Italian botanist working in Warsaw, packs a glass column with calcium carbonate powder. He pours a green plant extract through it, then rinses with petroleum ether. The single green mixture separates into distinct coloured bands as components travel down the column at different rates.

He calls the technique chromatography ('colour writing'). He uses it to identify multiple chlorophylls and carotenoids.

quote.text: Like light rays in the spectrum, so the different components of a pigment mixture are resolved on the calcium carbonate column.
quote.attrib: Mikhail Tswett, 1906

moments.takeaway: Different molecules interact differently with a solid; this is enough to separate them. A new and powerful tool.

moments.title: Chromatography ignored
moments.body:
Tswett's papers are mostly in Russian. The mainstream chemistry community largely ignores them. Some leading chemists deny that the technique works at all.

Tswett dies of starvation in 1919 during the Russian Civil War. His method is rediscovered around 1930 by Kuhn and Lederer in Germany, applied to carotenoids, and finally enters mainstream use.
moments.takeaway: Language barriers and academic gatekeeping can delay technique adoption by decades.

moments.title: Partition chromatography and amino acid analysis
moments.who: Archer Martin and Richard Synge, Leeds
moments.body:
Martin and Synge invent partition chromatography (using a stationary liquid film, not just solid adsorbent) and apply it to amino acid mixtures. They get a 1952 Nobel Prize.

Their technique made amino acid composition analysis tractable. Without it, Sanger's sequencing of insulin (1955) and the subsequent revolution in protein chemistry could not have happened.
moments.takeaway: Chromatography becomes a precision tool for biology, not just plant pigments.

moments.title: HPLC and GC dominate analytical labs
moments.body:
High-pressure (now 'high-performance') liquid chromatography, gas chromatography and gas-chromatography-mass-spectrometry become the workhorses of analytical chemistry. Every drug, every environmental sample, every metabolite assay relies on some form of chromatography.

Reversed-phase HPLC (silica with C18 chains) becomes the standard separation method for organic small molecules.
moments.takeaway: Tswett's coloured bands on a calcium carbonate column become a 100-billion-dollar industry.

now.title: Chromatography today
now.body:
Chromatography is the backbone of nearly all analytical, pharmaceutical and environmental chemistry. HPLC routinely separates thousands of compounds in proteomics workflows. Mass spec coupled with chromatography identifies and quantifies trace species at femtogram levels.

New formats: UHPLC (sub-2 micron particles, 1000+ bar pressures), supercritical fluid chromatography (CO2 mobile phase), ion-mobility spectrometry-MS (separates by shape AND mass).
now.open_questions: Can chromatography be miniaturised to lab-on-a-chip scale for clinical point-of-care? Can machine learning select optimal separation conditions automatically? Can we achieve full single-cell metabolomics with chromatographic detection?

items.reflection: Tswett invented modern chromatography in 1903 and died in obscurity. His method was rediscovered, claimed independently, and revolutionised chemistry — without him being widely credited until decades after his death. How should a discipline honour earlier work that was overlooked or dismissed?

moments.title: Dalton begins his atomic notes
moments.body:
Dalton, a Quaker schoolmaster with no university post, begins keeping notebooks on gases and meteorology. He notes that gases in a mixture exert pressure independently (Dalton's law of partial pressures) and starts to think the gases are made of discrete particles of fixed mass.

He presents his ideas at the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society in 1803.
moments.takeaway: A working-class teacher, in his evening notes, lays the basis of modern atomic theory.

moments.title: A New System of Chemical Philosophy
moments.body:
Dalton publishes the first volume of A New System of Chemical Philosophy. He proposes: all matter is made of atoms; atoms of an element are identical in mass; atoms of different elements differ in mass; compounds form by combining atoms in fixed integer ratios.

His evidence is the law of multiple proportions: carbon and oxygen form CO and CO2 with mass ratios 1:1.33 and 1:2.67 respectively — neat whole-number ratios that imply discrete combining units.

quote.text: We might as well attempt to introduce a new planet into the solar system, or annihilate one already in existence, as to create or destroy a particle of hydrogen.
quote.attrib: John Dalton, A New System of Chemical Philosophy, 1808

moments.takeaway: The first quantitative atomic theory. Dalton's atoms are indivisible — and that part he gets wrong, a century later.

moments.title: Brown observes random motion of pollen
moments.body:
Botanist Robert Brown observes pollen grains in water under a microscope and notes their incessant random jiggling. He cannot explain it. The 'Brownian motion' lacks an accepted mechanism for nearly 80 years.

In 1905 Einstein analyses Brownian motion mathematically, showing it arises from water molecules' random thermal impacts on the pollen. Perrin (1908) confirms experimentally. Atoms move from inference to direct observation.
moments.takeaway: Atoms are real, measurable objects — not just bookkeeping conveniences. Confirmation comes a century after Dalton.

moments.title: Dalton dies, mourned by Manchester
moments.body:
Dalton dies aged 77, having never held a university post. His funeral procession is followed by 40,000 mourners through Manchester. His body lies in state at the Town Hall and is viewed by tens of thousands.

He was colour-blind — he wrote the first scientific account of the condition, which was called 'Daltonism' for a century. He never saw the yellow flame of sodium because he couldn't see yellow.
moments.takeaway: An outsider's quiet work changed chemistry forever. He died revered by his city but never knighted, never academic-honoured at scale.

now.title: Atomic theory today
now.body:
Dalton's indivisible atoms have been split (Thomson 1897 — electron; Rutherford 1909 — nucleus; Chadwick 1932 — neutron) and further split (quarks — Friedman, Kendall and Taylor 1968). His insistence on discrete combining units in fixed integer ratios remains correct and is the foundation of stoichiometry.

We now image single atoms (STM 1981), manipulate them (optical tweezers — Ashkin, 2018 Nobel), and use them as quantum bits (trapped ion quantum computers).
now.open_questions: Is there a deeper structure below quarks? Why are there three families of fundamental particles? Why are mass ratios between fundamental particles what they are?

items.reflection: Dalton's atoms turned out to be divisible after all — yet his framework survives essentially intact. How is it possible for a theory to be wrong in its central premise (indivisibility) and yet remain a working foundation for an entire discipline?

moments.title: Mendeleev arranges 63 elements by atomic mass
moments.body:
Mendeleev, 35 years old, is writing a chemistry textbook (Principles of Chemistry). To organise his material, he writes the 63 known elements on cards and arranges them by atomic mass. He notices similar properties recur regularly.

He publishes a table in the Journal of the Russian Chemical Society on 6 March 1869. Where his pattern needs an element that doesn't exist, he LEAVES A GAP.
moments.takeaway: A textbook organisational scheme becomes a fundamental scientific theory.

moments.title: Mendeleev predicts eka-silicon
moments.body:
In a more detailed second paper, Mendeleev predicts the properties of three then-unknown elements he calls eka-boron, eka-aluminium and eka-silicon. For eka-silicon he predicts: atomic mass ~72, density ~5.5 g/cm3, grey metal, oxide formula MO2 with density ~4.7 g/cm3, chloride MCl4 boiling under 100°C.

Most chemists treat the predictions sceptically.

quote.text: We must expect the discovery of many yet unknown elements — for example, two analogues of boron and aluminium with atomic weights 65 and 75.
quote.attrib: Mendeleev, 1871

moments.takeaway: A theory makes specific, testable predictions about substances no one has yet held in their hand.

moments.title: Gallium, scandium, germanium found
moments.body:
Lecoq de Boisbaudran isolates gallium in 1875 (eka-aluminium). Properties match Mendeleev's predictions almost exactly. Nilson isolates scandium in 1879 (eka-boron) — also a match.

In 1886 Clemens Winkler isolates germanium from argyrodite ore. Measured properties: atomic mass 72.6 (predicted 72), density 5.32 (predicted 5.5), grey metal, GeO2 density 4.7, GeCl4 boils at 86°C. Three predictions confirmed in 17 years.
moments.takeaway: The match converts scepticism into acceptance. The periodic table is now a scientific theory, not a classification.

moments.title: Mendeleev loses Nobel Prize by one vote
moments.body:
Mendeleev is nominated for the 1906 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The committee initially recommends him. But Svante Arrhenius (Nobel Committee member, and reportedly with a personal grudge after Mendeleev had criticised his electrolytic theory) campaigns hard against him. The vote tips to Henri Moissan (for isolating fluorine) by one vote.

Mendeleev dies in 1907 without a Nobel. Element 101 (mendelevium) is named after him in 1955.
moments.takeaway: Scientific recognition is shaped by politics, rivalry and timing — not only by merit.

now.title: The periodic table today
now.body:
118 elements are confirmed; the last (oganesson, Z=118) was named in 2016. Superheavy element synthesis happens at heavy-ion colliders in Dubna (Russia), GSI (Germany) and RIKEN (Japan), one or a few atoms at a time.

Quantum mechanics now explains the table's structure: shells, subshells, electron configurations and the Pauli principle. Mendeleev's empirical patterns are direct consequences of orbital filling rules.
now.open_questions: How far can the table extend? Predictions of an 'island of stability' near Z=114 or Z=126 suggest some superheavy nuclei could be relatively long-lived. Searches for element 119 have been running since 2007 with no confirmed result.

items.reflection: Mendeleev's table worked even though he had no idea atoms had electron shells — he was inferring quantum mechanics from chemical behaviour 50 years before quantum mechanics existed. How do scientists build accurate models of phenomena whose underlying mechanism is still unknown?

moments.title: Becquerel discovers radioactivity
moments.body:
Becquerel had been testing whether phosphorescent uranium salts emit X-rays after sunlight exposure. Cloudy weather forces him to put the experiment in a drawer. He develops the plates anyway and finds them exposed.

Uranium emits its own penetrating radiation, with no sunlight needed. The phenomenon is later named 'radioactivity' by Marie Curie.
moments.takeaway: An accidental cloudy day leads to a fundamental discovery. Some elements spontaneously emit radiation.

moments.title: Marie and Pierre Curie isolate polonium and radium
moments.who: Marie Skłodowska Curie and Pierre Curie, Paris
moments.body:
Marie Curie, looking for a PhD topic, picks up Becquerel's work. Using an electrometer Pierre and his brother had designed, she measures radioactivity quantitatively. She notices pitchblende is more radioactive than its uranium content alone could explain — there must be a more radioactive element in it.

Over four years, the Curies process tonnes of pitchblende in a leaky shed at the rue Lhomond in Paris, in Parisian winters. They isolate two new elements: polonium (July 1898, named for Poland) and radium (December 1898).

quote.text: Radium ought to enrich no one. It is an element; it belongs to the people.
quote.attrib: Marie Curie, on refusing to patent the isolation process

moments.takeaway: Two new elements isolated from tonnes of ore by hand, in a shed, with no research budget — and freely shared with the world.

moments.title: First Nobel — physics
moments.body:
The Nobel Committee in Stockholm initially names only Becquerel and Pierre. Pierre writes refusing to accept unless Marie is included. The committee yields.

Marie Curie becomes the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. She and Pierre are too ill from radiation exposure to travel to Stockholm to accept it in person.
moments.takeaway: The first formal recognition of radioactivity — and of one of its discoverers as a woman in a male-dominated field.

moments.title: Second Nobel — chemistry
moments.body:
Pierre died in 1906 (run over by a horse-drawn cart on a Paris street). Marie continues alone. In 1911 she wins a second Nobel Prize, in Chemistry, for her isolation of pure radium metal.

She is still the only person to have won Nobels in two different sciences. The same year she is denied election to the French Academy of Sciences by a single vote — partly because she is a woman, partly because she is foreign, partly because the press had recently scandalised her relationship with the physicist Paul Langevin.
moments.takeaway: Two Nobels, a denied Academy seat. Recognition is uneven even at the highest level.

now.title: Radioactive elements today
now.body:
Polonium and radium are now well understood — both decay by alpha emission, with radium having a half-life of 1600 years and polonium-210 having a half-life of 138 days. Radium was used in glow-in-the-dark watch dials (the 'Radium Girls' factory workers in the 1910s-1920s died of jaw cancer from licking their brushes) until its danger became clear.

We now know about 3000 isotopes of 118 elements. Radioactive isotopes are used in medical imaging (PET, SPECT), therapy (cobalt-60, iodine-131), and dating (carbon-14, uranium-lead).
now.open_questions: Why are some isotope half-lives 1 second and others 10 to the 19 years? What's the upper limit on element half-life for superheavy nuclei? How safely can the long-lived components of nuclear waste be managed over geological time?

items.reflection: Marie Curie died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia, almost certainly from her decades of radiation exposure. She kept radium in her desk drawer. Her notebooks are still so radioactive they are stored in lead boxes. What does it say about scientific discovery that the dangers were only learned at the cost of the discoverers' lives?

moments.title: Rutherford notices alpha deflections
moments.body:
Rutherford had won the 1908 Nobel Prize for his work on radioactive decay. He notices that when alpha particles pass through thin foils they are sometimes deflected through small angles.

The plum pudding model of the atom (Thomson's, with positive charge spread out and electrons embedded) predicts at most very small deflections. Rutherford asks his colleagues Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden to look more carefully.
moments.takeaway: An observation 'in the noise' becomes the seed of a revolution.

moments.title: Geiger and Marsden see backscatter
moments.who: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, Manchester
moments.body:
Geiger and Marsden, working under Rutherford, fire alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most pass through with small deflections. About 1 in 8000 bounce back nearly opposite to the direction they came from.

Rutherford later described his reaction: 'It was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.'

quote.text: It was quite the most incredible event that has ever happened to me in my life.
quote.attrib: Ernest Rutherford, recollection of the gold foil result

moments.takeaway: Backscatter is impossible if positive charge is spread out. Something tiny and dense must be deflecting alpha particles.

moments.title: Rutherford's nuclear atom
moments.body:
Rutherford publishes his nuclear model of the atom. Positive charge and most of the mass sit in a tiny central nucleus, with radius less than 10 to the minus 14 m. Electrons orbit at relatively huge distance (about 10 to the minus 10 m). The atom is mostly empty space.

The plum pudding model dies. The Rutherford model has its own problem (orbiting electrons should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, classically). Bohr fixes this in 1913 with quantised orbits.
moments.takeaway: The atom has internal structure dominated by a tiny central body. Atomic mass is almost entirely nuclear.

moments.title: First artificial nuclear transmutation
moments.body:
Rutherford bombards nitrogen-14 with alpha particles and detects protons. The alpha + nitrogen reaction has transmuted nitrogen-14 into oxygen-17 plus a proton.

This is the first artificial nuclear reaction. Atoms can be changed from one element to another by nuclear bombardment.
moments.takeaway: Alchemy fulfilled — by nuclear physics. Elements are not permanent; they can be transmuted by bombardment.

now.title: Inside the nucleus today
now.body:
We know the nucleus contains protons and neutrons, themselves made of quarks bound by gluons (quantum chromodynamics). The Rutherford-style scattering experiment is the basic technique for probing nuclear and subnuclear structure — at higher energies it became deep inelastic scattering, which revealed quarks at SLAC in 1968.

Nuclear properties are catalogued in the National Nuclear Data Center and similar; nuclear physics is mature enough for engineering applications (medical isotopes, reactors, weapons).
now.open_questions: What is the precise structure of the nucleon (proton and neutron)? Can stable superheavy elements exist near a hypothetical 'island of stability'? How do nuclei behave in neutron stars at supranuclear densities?

items.reflection: Rutherford was a chemist by his Nobel and a physicist by his work. He famously remarked: 'In science there is only physics; all the rest is stamp collecting.' His ribbing of chemistry came from someone who won the chemistry Nobel. How does the territory between disciplines get carved up by personalities and conventions?

moments.title: Pauling introduces resonance and hybridisation
moments.body:
Pauling publishes a paper in the Journal of the American Chemical Society titled 'The Nature of the Chemical Bond. Application of Results Obtained from the Quantum Mechanics and from a Theory of Paramagnetic Susceptibility to the Structure of Molecules.'

He introduces the concept of hybridised atomic orbitals (sp, sp2, sp3) and resonance between Lewis structures. Both ideas become standard chemistry within a decade.
moments.takeaway: Quantum mechanics is brought into structural chemistry. Bonding becomes describable in orbital language.

moments.title: Electronegativity scale
moments.body:
Pauling derives a numerical scale of electronegativity from bond dissociation energies. The most electronegative element (fluorine) gets 4.0; the least (caesium) about 0.7. Differences in electronegativity predict bond polarity quantitatively.

The scale becomes universal. Every chemistry textbook still uses Pauling electronegativity values.
moments.takeaway: A simple number summarises a deep chemical property. Electronegativity becomes a workhorse of structural prediction.

moments.title: The Nature of the Chemical Bond (book)
moments.body:
Pauling publishes the book version of his ideas: The Nature of the Chemical Bond. It integrates resonance, hybridisation, electronegativity, partial ionic character and crystal structure into one framework. It becomes one of the most-cited science books of the 20th century.

The book is still in print and is the foundation of how chemists talk about bonds today.

quote.text: The chemical bond, as we now know, is the most important thing in molecular structure.
quote.attrib: Linus Pauling, The Nature of the Chemical Bond, 1939

moments.takeaway: A single book systematises bonding for the entire field. Generations of chemists learn from it.

moments.title: Two Nobel Prizes
moments.body:
Pauling wins the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry 'for his research into the nature of the chemical bond.' He is the sole recipient.

In 1962 he wins the Nobel Peace Prize for his campaign against atmospheric nuclear weapons testing. He had personally lobbied governments and gathered signatures from over 11,000 scientists. The 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty was partly the result. He remains one of only four people to win two Nobel Prizes — and the only one to have won both unshared.
moments.takeaway: Two Nobels, in different fields, both unshared. A scientist's public conscience can also be world-changing.

now.title: Bonding theory today
now.body:
Pauling's valence bond theory coexists with molecular orbital theory, which is generally more accurate for delocalised systems. Modern computational chemistry uses density functional theory (DFT) and ab initio methods to predict bond properties from first principles.

Electronegativity remains a useful concept, though it has been redefined several times (Mulliken, Allred-Rochow, Allen) on different theoretical bases. Pauling's empirical values still appear in most textbooks.
now.open_questions: Can DFT functionals be designed to handle all bonds correctly without empirical adjustment? How well can we predict properties of materials and biomolecules from quantum mechanics alone? Are there bond types that still resist quantum-mechanical description?

items.reflection: Pauling's later years included a famous wrong turn — his unshakeable advocacy of high-dose vitamin C as a cure for everything from colds to cancer, which clinical trials repeatedly failed to support. A great scientist can still be powerfully wrong. How should the discipline weigh a lifetime's achievement against late-career errors?

moments.title: Vital force is established doctrine
moments.body:
Most chemists hold that organic compounds — those found in living things — require a 'vital force' to be made. You can analyse and decompose them in the lab but you cannot synthesise them from inorganic precursors. The boundary between living and non-living chemistry seems sharp.

Berzelius (the most influential chemist of the era) articulates the position formally.
moments.takeaway: The chemistry of life is held to be inaccessible to laboratory synthesis.

moments.title: Wöhler accidentally makes urea
moments.body:
Wöhler is trying to make ammonium cyanate (NH4OCN) by combining silver cyanate and ammonium chloride. The product crystallises as colourless prisms with melting point 132°C — identical to urea (CO(NH2)2), the organic compound excreted by mammalian kidneys.

He writes to Berzelius: 'I must tell you that I can prepare urea without requiring a kidney of an animal, either man or dog. Ammonium cyanate is urea.'

quote.text: I must tell you that I can prepare urea without requiring a kidney of an animal, either man or dog.
quote.attrib: Friedrich Wöhler, letter to Jöns Jakob Berzelius, 22 February 1828

moments.takeaway: An organic substance — urea — is made from inorganic precursors. The vital force doctrine takes its first hit.

moments.title: More syntheses pile up
moments.body:
Hermann Kolbe synthesises acetic acid from carbon disulfide and chlorine (1845) — a more complex organic molecule made from purely inorganic sources.

Marcellin Berthelot synthesises methanol, ethanol, methane, ethyne and benzene from inorganic precursors during the 1850s and 1860s. He publishes Chimie Organique Fondée sur la Synthèse in 1860 — a deliberate manifesto against vitalism.

By 1870 vitalism is no longer scientifically respectable.
moments.takeaway: Vitalism doesn't die in one moment. It erodes under accumulating evidence over decades.

moments.title: Miller-Urey: amino acids from a primitive atmosphere
moments.who: Stanley Miller and Harold Urey, University of Chicago
moments.body:
Miller (then a graduate student) and Urey simulate Earth's early atmosphere: methane, ammonia, hydrogen, water, with electric discharges as 'lightning'. After a week the water turns brown. Analysis shows glycine, alanine and other amino acids.

Not just organic compounds — biological building blocks — can form from purely inorganic mixtures.
moments.takeaway: Origin-of-life chemistry becomes an experimental subject. The boundary between living and non-living chemistry vanishes.

now.title: Organic chemistry today
now.body:
Organic synthesis is a dominant branch of chemistry. Total syntheses of complex natural products (vitamin B12 — Woodward and Eschenmoser 1973, palytoxin — Kishi 1994, vancomycin — Evans, Boger and Nicolaou 1998-1999) showcase what is possible.

AI-assisted retrosynthesis (e.g. IBM RXN, Chematica/Synthia) now matches or exceeds expert chemists at planning routes.
now.open_questions: Can life itself be synthesised from scratch? Craig Venter's group built a synthetic genome in 2010 and a minimal synthetic cell (JCVI-syn3.0) in 2016. Full de novo synthesis of a living cell remains a goal. What chemistry occurs on Titan, Enceladus, or in protoplanetary disks?

items.reflection: Wöhler's 1828 letter to Berzelius is often presented as the single death-blow to vitalism. Historians of science have argued the reality was much more gradual. How does the human desire for tidy 'revolution moments' shape the stories we tell about science?

moments.title: Biot discovers optical activity
moments.body:
Biot finds that solutions of certain organic compounds (turpentine, sugar, tartaric acid) rotate the plane of polarised light. The phenomenon is reproducible but unexplained.

Biot is unable to connect the rotation to any structural feature of the molecules. He suspects but cannot prove that asymmetric molecules are responsible.
moments.takeaway: An odd optical phenomenon waits for an explanation.

moments.title: Pasteur separates tartrate crystals by hand
moments.who: Louis Pasteur, École Normale Supérieure, Paris
moments.body:
Pasteur, aged 26, is studying sodium ammonium tartrate. He notices the crystals come in two mirror-image (hemihedral) forms. Using a hand lens and tweezers, he sorts them into two piles.

A solution of one pile rotates polarised light to the right; the other to the left. Combined, they cancel exactly. He has separated the first known pair of enantiomers.

quote.text: Tout est trouvé! (Everything is solved!)
quote.attrib: Louis Pasteur, reportedly on separating the crystals

moments.takeaway: A young chemist discovers chirality with tools no more sophisticated than tweezers and a hand lens.

moments.title: Pasteur connects chirality to life
moments.body:
Pasteur proposes that life is intrinsically chiral. Natural sources produce only one enantiomer of tartaric acid (the (+) form); the racemic mixture only appears when chemists make it synthetically.

He ferments racemic tartrate with mould (Penicillium glaucum) and shows the mould consumes only one enantiomer, leaving the other untouched. Biology can distinguish what physics cannot.
moments.takeaway: Biological systems are intrinsically homochiral. Life chooses one hand over the other.

moments.title: Van 't Hoff and Le Bel: tetrahedral carbon
moments.who: Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff (Utrecht) and Joseph Achille Le Bel (Paris) — independently
moments.body:
Van 't Hoff and Le Bel propose that the four bonds of carbon point to the corners of a tetrahedron. Carbons with four different groups are intrinsically chiral, with two non-superposable mirror images.

The paper structural foundation of stereochemistry is laid. Van 't Hoff goes on to win the first ever Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1901), partly for this work.
moments.takeaway: The molecular geometry behind chirality is identified. Stereochemistry becomes a structural science.

now.title: Chirality today
now.body:
Biology is overwhelmingly homochiral: all natural proteins use L-amino acids; all natural DNA and RNA use D-sugars. Many drugs are chiral and only one enantiomer is active; the other may be inactive or harmful.

The thalidomide tragedy (1957-1962) drove home the importance: one enantiomer treated morning sickness, the other caused severe limb birth defects in babies. Even worse, thalidomide racemises in vivo, so giving a pure enantiomer doesn't help.

Modern pharma uses asymmetric synthesis (Sharpless, Noyori, Knowles — 2001 Nobel) and chiral chromatography routinely.
now.open_questions: Why is biology homochiral? Hypotheses include parity violation in weak decay, circularly polarised light from neutron stars and other autocatalytic prebiotic mechanisms — but no one knows for certain. Has any extraterrestrial chiral biology been detected (e.g. in meteorites)? Slight excesses of one enantiomer have been found in Murchison and similar meteorites.

items.reflection: Pasteur sorted crystals with tweezers — a low-tech experiment with deep consequences for biology, chemistry and pharmacy. How often do major discoveries come from patient hands-on work that anyone with eyes and a tweezers could have done — if they had thought to look?

moments.title: C60 detected in a vacuum chamber
moments.who: Harold Kroto (Sussex), Robert Curl and Richard Smalley (Rice University)
moments.body:
Kroto visits Smalley's lab in Houston in September 1985. Smalley has built a laser-vaporisation apparatus to study clusters of refractory atoms. Kroto wants to simulate carbon-chain chemistry in red giant stars.

They vaporise graphite. The mass spectrum shows a strong peak at mass 720 — exactly 60 carbon atoms. After 11 days of work, they propose the structure: a hollow truncated icosahedron with 12 pentagonal and 20 hexagonal faces — a soccer ball.
moments.takeaway: A new pure form of carbon, with a soccer-ball structure, appears in a vacuum chamber.

moments.title: Krätschmer-Huffman bulk synthesis
moments.body:
Krätschmer and Huffman find that vaporising graphite electrodes in helium produces bulk quantities of C60 — extractable as a red-brown solution in benzene.

Before this, C60 had only been made in fleeting amounts in vacuum chambers. Now any lab can buy or make grams of it. Research explodes worldwide.
moments.takeaway: Bulk synthesis turns a curiosity into a research subject.

moments.title: Carbon nanotubes
moments.body:
Iijima examines soot from a Krätschmer-style arc by electron microscopy and finds long cylindrical structures: rolled-up graphene sheets capped at the ends — carbon nanotubes.

The nanotubes have remarkable properties: extreme tensile strength (about 100 GPa, stronger than steel by mass), high thermal conductivity, and electronic properties that depend on the rolling angle (metallic or semiconducting).
moments.takeaway: Hollow carbon structures extend from soccer balls to cylinders. A whole class of nanocarbons is opened.

moments.title: Graphene isolated
moments.who: Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov, University of Manchester
moments.body:
Geim and Novoselov use Scotch tape to peel layers from graphite repeatedly until they get single one-atom-thick sheets — graphene. A material previously considered theoretically impossible as an isolated 2D crystal turns out to be remarkably stable.

Graphene has extraordinary electronic properties (electrons behave as massless Dirac fermions), enormous tensile strength, and high transparency. They win the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.
moments.takeaway: The last major carbon allotrope is isolated using office tape. A 2D form of carbon now exists in the lab.

now.title: Carbon nanomaterials today
now.body:
Fullerenes, carbon nanotubes and graphene form a research field of their own. Applications include batteries, solar cells, transparent electrodes, structural composites, biological sensors and drug delivery vehicles.

C60 has since been detected in space — in the interstellar medium (Cami et al., 2010) and in supernova remnants — solving an 85-year-old mystery about 'diffuse interstellar bands' in stellar spectra.
now.open_questions: Can carbon nanotube fibres be made in macroscopic lengths without defects? Can graphene transistors compete with silicon for computing? Why does C60 form so readily in carbon-rich plasmas — both lab and stellar?

items.reflection: Kroto, Curl and Smalley were not looking for a new allotrope of carbon. They were studying interstellar molecules. A whole new class of materials emerged from a question about astrochemistry. How often do scientific discoveries solve problems different from the ones the researchers set out to solve?

moments.title: Perkin tries to make quinine
moments.who: William Henry Perkin, Royal College of Chemistry, London
moments.body:
William Perkin is an 18-year-old chemistry student in August Wilhelm von Hofmann's lab. Hofmann had speculated about synthesising quinine (the antimalarial extracted from cinchona bark) from coal tar derivatives.

Over the Easter holiday, Perkin works in his home laboratory (a board over the bath). He oxidises aniline (a coal-tar derivative) with potassium dichromate. He gets a black tarry sludge. Washing it with alcohol gives a brilliant purple solution.

He has not made quinine. He has made the first synthetic organic dye — mauveine.
moments.takeaway: A failed undergraduate synthesis produces a new dye. Industrial chemistry has its founding accident.

moments.title: Perkin files a patent and builds a factory
moments.body:
Perkin (still 18, technically a minor) recognises the commercial potential. He files a patent in August 1856. With his father and brother, he sets up the first synthetic dyestuffs factory at Greenford, just west of London.

The dye is launched as 'Tyrian purple', then renamed 'mauve' after the French for the mallow flower. Queen Victoria wears mauve to her daughter's wedding in 1858. The colour explodes across European fashion.
moments.takeaway: A teenager builds a chemical industry from scratch using a serendipitous result.

moments.title: German synthetic dye industry overtakes Britain
moments.body:
German chemists and industrialists build on Perkin's discovery far more systematically. By the 1880s, BASF, Hoechst, Bayer and Agfa dominate synthetic dye production worldwide.

The research tradition spreads from dyes to pharmaceuticals: aspirin (Bayer 1899), Salvarsan (Ehrlich 1909, the first chemotherapeutic for syphilis), Prontosil (the first sulfa antibiotic, 1932) all come from the dye-research culture.
moments.takeaway: Industrial chemistry concentrates in Germany. By 1900, German organic chemistry dominates the world.

moments.title: Perkin's 50th anniversary celebration
moments.who: Society of Chemical Industry, London and New York
moments.body:
Perkin is honoured worldwide. He receives the first Perkin Medal in 1906 (still awarded annually in the United States) and is knighted by King Edward VII in 1906. He dies in 1907.

His Greenford factory site is now a residential estate; a blue plaque marks his discovery's role.
moments.takeaway: An accidental discovery created a multibillion-pound industry over a single human lifetime.

now.title: Synthetic dyes and downstream chemistry today
now.body:
Synthetic dyes — and the broader synthetic chemistry tradition they founded — underpin pharmaceuticals, plastics, photography, agrochemicals and modern colour printing. The IUPAC Colour Index lists thousands of synthetic dyes.

Mauveine itself has long been replaced by cheaper and more colourfast purples (notably methyl violet and similar triphenylmethane dyes). But the chemistry tradition Perkin started endures.
now.open_questions: Can chemistry replace petroleum-based dye precursors with sustainable bio-based feedstocks? Can dye chemistry be redirected to functional materials (OLED emitters, dye-sensitised solar cells, photodynamic therapy agents)?

items.reflection: Perkin retired wealthy at 36 to focus on pure research. His 'failure' to make quinine gave him a fortune and gave the world a colour-and-pharma industry. How should we judge scientific failures that turn out to be more important than the goals they failed at?

moments.title: Pauling predicts noble gas compounds
moments.body:
Pauling speculates that the heavier noble gases — krypton, xenon, radon — should be able to form compounds with fluorine. He suggests XeF6 and KrF6 should exist.

No one tries seriously. The experimental challenges are formidable: fluorine is dangerous, xenon is expensive, and the experimental consensus says noble gases don't react.
moments.takeaway: A theoretical prediction sits unexamined for nearly 30 years.

moments.title: Bartlett notices a match of ionisation energies
moments.who: Neil Bartlett, University of British Columbia
moments.body:
Bartlett is working with platinum hexafluoride (PtF6), an extraordinarily strong oxidiser. He notices a sample turns red on contact with air. Analysis: PtF6 has stripped an electron from O2, giving O2+ PtF6-.

He looks up the relevant ionisation energies: O2 is 1175 kJ/mol; xenon is 1170 kJ/mol. Almost the same. He reasons that PtF6 should also be able to oxidise xenon.
moments.takeaway: An almost-coincidental match of two numbers points to a new chemistry.

moments.title: The first noble gas compound
moments.who: Neil Bartlett, University of British Columbia
moments.body:
On 23 March 1962 (later widely reported as June 1962 when the paper appeared), Bartlett combines xenon gas with PtF6 vapour in a glass apparatus. The reaction is instantaneous — a yellow solid forms.

He characterises it as Xe+[PtF6]- (later shown to be more complex). The first compound of a noble gas exists.

quote.text: I had to look twice to believe it.
quote.attrib: Neil Bartlett, on the first XePtF6 product

moments.takeaway: The 'inert gases' are not entirely inert. A six-decade-old chemistry orthodoxy falls.

moments.title: An entire new chemistry opens
moments.who: Argonne, Oak Ridge, Berkeley and others
moments.body:
Within months, Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne produce XeF4 by simply heating xenon with fluorine at 400°C in a nickel container. XeF2 (Hoppe, Münster) and XeF6 (Slivnik, Ljubljana) follow within two years.

XeO3 (an explosive oxide), KrF2 and ClO3+ F- soon follow. The full set of compounds maps the noble gases' chemistry from element 36 (krypton) onwards.
moments.takeaway: A whole chemistry — written off as impossible — opens up in two years.

now.title: Noble gas chemistry today
now.body:
Xenon and krypton have rich chemistry: oxides, fluorides, oxyfluorides and even Xe-N, Xe-C bonded compounds. Radon is too radioactive to study extensively but is known to form RnF2. Argon forms HArF only at cryogenic temperatures (Helsinki, 2000).

Xenon difluoride is used as a selective oxidising/fluorinating agent in organic synthesis. Excimer lasers (KrF, ArF, XeCl) use noble gas chemistry to produce intense UV light.
